description: Equipo multidisciplinario para afrontar nuevas retos
summary: On a mission to Mars, a message to the flight surgeon can take up to 22 minutes each way and evacuation is impossible: the crew must detect, interpret and act on their own health. VIGÍA (Spanish for "lookout") is an offline-first web app that tells each astronaut how they are and what to do next, without waiting for Earth. It compares each astronaut with their own baseline, not with an average patient. Gather: a guided daily check-in (heart rate, blood pressure, SpO2, temperature, sleep, mood, symptoms, weekly glucose). Evaluate: a three-layer engine checks each reading against clinical safety bands, the astronaut's own baseline and slow drifts, and joins it with real NASA and NOAA environment data (DONKI solar particle events, OSDR radiation dose and cabin CO2, GOES proton flux). Act: a 3D body shows green, amber or red per system with the reason and the next step; only a red safety alert reaches the crew medical officer. We tested the engine on 780 synthetic missions and publish the failures too: it caught 60 of 60 intense drifts but only 1 of 60 subtle ones. Research prototype for decision support, not a medical device; professional and clinical validation are pending.
details: Team ex umbra in solem (Concepción, Chile): Sebastián Morales, Ignacio Castillo, Fernando Marihuen, Josecarlos Vidal. Live app: https://vigia.smoraleslo.dev/?modo=demo&lang=en . WHAT IT DOES. VIGÍA is the on-board health companion of a long-duration crew. Each astronaut completes a daily check-in: resting heart rate, systolic blood pressure, SpO2, temperature, sleep, mood, a closed list of symptoms and, weekly, glucose. Each indicator has a fact sheet built from NASA Human Research Program material. A Galaxy Watch4 can pre-fill heart rate and SpO2. HOW IT DECIDES. A hybrid engine (Python reference and TypeScript app, with a parity test) asks three questions. Layer A, clinical safety: a partial adaptation of NEWS2 bands for the four parameters we capture, with our own cut-offs; it is not the full NEWS2 and its validation does not transfer to this prototype. Layer B, personal deviation: a modified z-score against the astronaut's own baseline, two days in a row. Layer C, slow drift: a one-sided CUSUM on heart rate, sleep and mood. Context rules: cabin CO2 above 3 mmHg with headache becomes a crew-level alert; a GOES proton flux of 10 pfu or more, or a NASA DONKI SEP event, switches storm mode on. OUTPUT. A clickable 3D body shows green, amber or red per system with the reason and next step. The Environment screen shows radiation dose, proton flux, SEP events and cabin CO2, each labelled Real or Simulated with source and date. Green and amber never leave the device; only a red alert reaches the crew medical officer with the minimum data. Reports travel to Earth under the communication delay. Everything works offline. DEMO MODE. A labelled simulated crew on a 259-day Earth-Mars transit, with the real DONKI solar particle events of 2011-2012 on their true dates. EVIDENCE, INCLUDING FAILURES. We ran the engine on 780 synthetic missions, 13 scenarios and 7 methods, with a frozen protocol. It detected 60 of 60 intense drifts (95% CI 94.0-100%) but only 1 of 60 subtle drifts (95% CI 0.3-8.9%); a personal-baseline comparator caught 4 of 60, so we do not claim superiority. This is a same-team exploratory benchmark, not a human cohort. Reference datasets with verified provenance: MMASH (22 terrestrial participants, PhysioNet) and one day of Artemis I / Orion radiation from NASA RadLab (four instruments). LIMITS. No real astronaut physiology is used; demo physiology is simulated. No professional review or clinical validation has been carried out yet. Not a medical device. TOOLS. Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, three.js, FastAPI, SQLite, Python; 373 automated tests. AI coding assistants (Claude Code, OpenAI Codex) helped with research, documentation, code, tests and synthetic benchmark cases; no AI-generated images, video or audio are used. We worked with the AI assistants through model-agnostic engineering practices, among them test-driven development (TDD) and spec-driven development (SDD): specifications and tests were written first and every change had to pass them. Source code and documentation: https://github.com/smoraleslo/vigia
